_docs.purpose: Single source of truth for the guide. The app derives the question count, order, numbering, colors, and every string from this file; nothing in the code assumes a particular number of questions.
editingRules: ballotOrderCertified: leave false until the Secretary of the Commonwealth certifies the order. While false, no question numbers are shown anywhere (no placeholders), and a notice banner appears on the overview.

draft: true shows the draft banner and turns on extra content linting in the browser console (missing shortTitle/yesMeans/noMeans/summary, missing ballotNumber while the order is certified). Set to false to publish.

fragmentSchemaVersion: BUMP THIS whenever the question list changes in count or order. The URL resume fragment (#s=...) encodes choices POSITIONALLY, so adding, removing, or reordering a question makes every previously shared link and printed QR mean the wrong thing. Bumping the version invalidates them explicitly instead of silently. Saved-on-device state is keyed by id and is unaffected.

id: stable, URL-safe slug. It is the storage key for a voter's saved answer, so DO NOT rename an id after publish — renaming discards that question's saved choice and note. Ids must be unique; duplicates are dropped with a console warning.

inverted: true for questions where a yes vote does the counterintuitive thing (e.g. a veto referendum). It triggers the 'Read this one carefully' callout and a compressed reminder on the ballot card. Optional companion field inversionShort supplies that short reminder text; otherwise it is derived from yesMeans.
accent: optional integer 1-9 to pin a question's identity color. Omit to cycle the palette by position.

fullGuide blocks: type is one of h2, h3, p, ul, ol, table. Unknown types are ignored, so new block types can be added to the renderer before content uses them. All text is inserted as plain text - HTML in strings will display as literal characters, not markup.
fiscal: null when there is no fiscal note; the line is hidden rather than showing an empty box.

meta.disclaimer: The Center for State Policy Analysis is nonpartisan and takes no position on any ballot question.

questions.officialTitle: A law revising the Chapter 62F tax-revenue cap and refund formula
summary: Chapter 62F, a 1986 law, returns money to taxpayers when state tax collections grow faster than wages and salaries. This measure would rebase that cap to the prior year's actual collections (grown by a three-year average of wage and salary growth) and fold in revenue from the millionaire surtax.

Supporters say the change makes refunds more frequent and larger and keeps government growth in check. Opponents group it with other anti-tax measures and warn it could constrain the state's ability to rebuild reserves after a downturn.
questions.yesMeans: Changes the Chapter 62F formula so tax-cap refunds are triggered more often and are larger.
questions.noMeans: Keeps the current 1986 Chapter 62F refund formula unchanged.
questions.fiscal: Analysts estimate the revised cap could have triggered several times in the past decade, redirecting billions of dollars to refunds.

fullGuide.text: Chapter 62F caps how much tax revenue the state may keep in a year. When collections exceed the cap, the excess is returned to taxpayers in proportion to what they paid. The cap last triggered a large refund in 2022.

items: The cap would be rebased to the prior year's actual collections rather than a 1986 baseline.
Growth would be indexed to a three-year average of wage and salary growth.
Revenue from the millionaire surtax would be counted toward the cap.

rows: In strong post-recession recovery years, the revised cap could hold collections below actual need.
The formula is technical, which is itself a liability for informed voting.

questions.officialTitle: An initiative to protect water and nature by dedicating existing sales-tax revenue
summary: This measure would dedicate the existing state sales tax collected on sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses to a new 'Nature for All Fund' — 50% at first, rising to 100% after July 1, 2028 — overseen by a 15-member board.

Because a ballot measure cannot itself appropriate money, the fund would remain subject to legislative appropriation. Supporters describe roughly $100 million per year 'without raising taxes'; critics note the Legislature could still fund it at zero.
questions.yesMeans: Dedicates existing sales-tax revenue from sporting goods and recreation to a conservation fund.
questions.noMeans: Leaves that sales-tax revenue in the state's general fund.
questions.fiscal: Coalition estimates about $100 million per year; the amount remains subject to legislative appropriation.

fullGuide.text: The measure directs a share of an existing tax stream into a dedicated fund rather than creating a new tax. The share rises from half to all of the relevant revenue after mid-2028.
A frequently raised point during committee hearings is that the fund is 'subject to appropriation,' meaning its practical effect depends on future legislative budgets.

questions.officialTitle: An initiative to allow single-family homes by right on small lots
summary: This measure would let single-family homes be built by right in any residentially zoned area on lots of at least 5,000 square feet with at least 50 feet of frontage and access to public water and sewer, overriding larger local minimum-lot requirements.
Supporters frame it as a housing-supply reform. Opponents cite local-control and infrastructure concerns, and note the measure sets a minimum lot size but places no cap on home size.
questions.yesMeans: Allows single-family homes by right on small lots statewide where public water and sewer exist.
questions.noMeans: Keeps existing local minimum-lot-size zoning rules.

fullGuide.text: 'By right' development can proceed without discretionary local permitting, so long as it meets the stated criteria.

items: The measure limits lot size but not home size.
The meaning of 'public water and sewer' access is not precisely defined.

questions.officialTitle: An initiative to establish a single all-candidate primary (top-two)
summary: This measure would replace separate party primaries for state, county, and congressional offices with a single all-candidate preliminary; the top two finishers advance to the general election. Presidential primaries and city elections are excluded.
Supporters argue it broadens choice and reduces polarization. Opponents, including both major state parties, question the evidence and note the potential for higher administrative costs.
questions.yesMeans: Replaces separate party primaries with one all-candidate primary; the top two advance.
questions.fiscal: Election administration costs would likely rise.

fullGuide.text: All candidates for an office appear on one preliminary ballot regardless of party. The two candidates with the most votes advance, which can mean two candidates of the same party in the general election.
